overview.title: 📖 Overview: Closing the Chapter on Intent, Opening the Laws of Blood
overview.subtitle: Keritot 20a–20b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf completes its exploration of intent and sequence in unwitting transgressions, testing whether performing two intended acts in reverse order still counts as fulfilling one's intent, using a memorable case of candles lit and extinguished in confusion. It then examines a famous dispute over one who stokes coals on Shabbat — extinguishing the upper coals while inadvertently igniting the lower ones — offering four different Amoraic explanations for why this might generate one or two sin offerings, each rooted in a different underlying tannaitic debate about intent and side-effects. With that, the chapter on uncertain and unintentional transgressions closes, and a new mishna opens: which types of blood, from which sources, carry the Torah's severe penalty of karet, and which are entirely exempt.

slides.title: 🕯️ Reversed Order — Does Intent Still Count?
slides.subtitle: A baraita about two burning candles tests Rava's theory of reversed sequence

lines.speaker: Rava's theory
lines.text: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua may disagree specifically about someone who intended to do two things in one order, but unwittingly did them in the REVERSE order.

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: Two candles are burning. He meant to extinguish THIS one but extinguished THAT one instead (or meant to light this one but lit that one) — exempt, since neither intended act was truly accomplished.

lines.speaker: Contrast case
lines.text: But if he meant to light one candle and then extinguish the other, and instead blew a single breath that did both simultaneously — liable, since his overall intention (one lit, one extinguished) was accomplished, even out of strict sequence.

lines.speaker: Why state the obvious?
lines.text: One might think: since he intended lighting FIRST and extinguishing SECOND, but they happened together, his intent wasn't truly fulfilled either way. The baraita teaches: since it didn't happen in reverse order either, the outcome still counts as fulfilling his intent.

callout.label: Underlying test:
callout.text: The precise sequencing of two intended results — not just their eventual accomplishment — can determine liability.

slides.title: 🔥 Four Ways to Explain 'Liable for Two'
slides.subtitle: Why does stoking coals (extinguishing the top, igniting the bottom) generate two sin offerings for one sage but not another?

boxes.title: R' Elazar & R' Ḥanina / R' Yoḥanan
items: A blacksmith wants only the top coals removed; igniting the bottom is an unwanted side-effect
Hinges on: is an undesired/destructive result of kindling still liable? (מְקַלְקֵל בְּהַבְעָרָה)

boxes.title: Ami bar Avin & R' Ḥananya bar Avin
items: He intended BOTH extinguishing and kindling
Hinges on: was kindling singled out in the Torah merely as an ordinary prohibition (Rabbi Yosei), or to divide labors and make each independently liable (Rabbi Natan)?

boxes.title: Rava
items: He intended to kindle FIRST, extinguish SECOND — but did them in reverse
Hinges on the same 'reversed order' principle as the candle case

boxes.title: Rav Ashi
items: He intended only to extinguish; the bottom coals ignited entirely on their own, unintended
Hinges on: is an unintended byproduct (דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין מִתְכַּוֵּין) liable (Rabbi Yehuda) or exempt (Rabbi Shimon)?

callout.label: One case, four frameworks:
callout.text: Each Amora locates the SAME two-offering ruling inside a completely different, independently attested tannaitic dispute — showing how many distinct legal principles govern intent on Shabbat.

slides.title: 🪵 Stoking for Warmth — When Self-Igniting Coals Divide the Sages
slides.subtitle: A parallel baraita on stoking coals purely to get warm, with the bottom coals catching fire unintentionally

nodes.content: 🔥 One stokes coals only to warm himself; the coals below ignite entirely on their own, with no intent at all
📜 One version of the baraita: LIABLE
💡 Reasoning: this tanna holds one IS liable for 'labor not needed for its own sake' (מְלָאכָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ צְרִיכָה לְגוּפָהּ) — even an incidental, unwanted result of a permitted action still counts
💡 Reasoning: this tanna holds one is NOT liable for labor not needed for its own sake — since the kindling served no purpose of his own, it doesn't count as prohibited labor

callout.label: Chapter closes here:
callout.text: With this dispute over intent and incidental labor, the chapter on uncertain and unintentional transgressions ("Safek Akhal Ḥelev") concludes.

slides.title: 🩸 Which Blood Carries Karet?
slides.subtitle: A new mishna opens: the Torah's blood prohibition, precisely sourced
rows: Blood that spurts during proper slaughter (domesticated, undomesticated, bird, kosher or not)
Blood from stabbing (neḥira) or maiming (ikur), or from bloodletting that removes the soul
Karet / sin offering — the soul departed through it
Blood of the spleen, heart, eggs, or grasshoppers
Exempt — not the blood that carries the life-force
Blood of exudate (oozing after the initial spurt of slaughter)
Exempt, per the first tanna; Rabbi Yehuda holds it IS liable

callout.label: Underlying principle:
callout.text: Only blood genuinely bound up with the departure of the life-force ('the soul departs through it') carries the Torah's severe penalty — blood that merely accompanies death without being its vehicle does not.

slides.title: 🐦 Excluding Human Blood — the Gemara's Comparison
slides.subtitle: How the Torah's phrase 'of bird or animal' narrows the scope of the blood prohibition

steps.content: 1️⃣ Leviticus 7:26: 'you shall consume no manner of blood' — read broadly, this could include human blood, egg blood, grasshopper blood, fish blood
2️⃣ The verse narrows it: 'whether it is of bird or of animal' — meaning only creatures sharing birds' and animals' defining features
3️⃣ Those shared features: capacity for BOTH light impurity (as food, if it becomes impure) AND severe impurity (as a corpse); capacity to be forbidden or permitted; and being a type of meat

4️⃣ Human beings are EXCLUDED: though a human corpse carries severe impurity, a living or dead human body never carries the 'light' food-impurity that applies to birds and animals — so human blood falls outside this prohibition

callout.label: Method:
callout.text: The Gemara isolates a precise set of shared halakhic traits from the verse's own comparative language, rather than reading the prohibition at its broadest possible scope.

summary.principle: Whether a Shabbat labor generates one liability, two, or none often turns on the precise relationship between intent and outcome — sequence, side-effects, and whether a labor serves the actor's actual purpose — while the Torah's blood prohibition is carefully bounded to the blood that genuinely carries away the life-force of birds and animals specifically.

flowSteps.content: 🕯️ A candle-lighting baraita shows that reversed order can exempt, but simultaneous fulfillment of intent still creates liability
🔥 Four Amoraim locate the coal-stoking dispute inside four distinct, independently known tannaitic debates about intent
🪵 A parallel dispute over self-igniting coals turns on whether incidental, purposeless labor is ever liable

columns.content: 🩸 The new mishna sorts blood sources into karet-liable and exempt categories
🐦 The Gemara excludes human blood by isolating the shared traits of 'bird or animal'

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: liability tracks precise legal criteria — sequence, purpose, and defining shared traits — never a surface-level reading of a prohibition's scope

quiz.q: According to the candle-lighting baraita, what happens if someone intends to extinguish one candle but accidentally extinguishes a different one instead?
o: He is liable, since a candle was extinguished either way
He is exempt, since his specific intended act was not accomplished
He must extinguish a third candle to atone
The ruling depends on the candle's size
quiz.e: The baraita rules he is exempt in this case, since his intent was for a specific candle, and that specific outcome was not achieved — unlike the case where his overall intention (one lit, one extinguished) was fulfilled simultaneously.

quiz.q: According to Rav Ashi's explanation of the two-sin-offerings dispute over stoking coals, what is the key underlying disagreement?
o: Whether coals can ever be considered fuel
Whether an unintended byproduct of an action (davar she'eino mitkavein) creates liability, disputed between Rabbi Yehuda (liable) and Rabbi Shimon (exempt)
Whether Shabbat labor requires two witnesses
Whether a blacksmith is exempt from all Shabbat laws
quiz.e: Rav Ashi locates the dispute in the debate between Rabbi Yehuda (who holds an unintended result of an action is still liable) and Rabbi Shimon (who holds it is exempt), applied to coals that ignite on their own without intent.

quiz.q: In the parallel baraita about stoking coals purely for warmth, where the lower coals ignite entirely on their own, what does the dispute between the two versions hinge on?
o: Whether coals can be moved on Shabbat at all
Whether one is liable for 'labor not needed for its own sake' (melakha she'eina tzericha legufah)
Whether warming oneself is ever permitted on Shabbat
Whether the coals were kosher
quiz.e: The two versions of the baraita reflect a dispute over whether performing a labor whose result serves no purpose of the actor's own (melakha she'eina tzericha legufah) creates liability.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, which type of blood is exempt from the Torah's karet penalty even though it comes from a properly slaughtered kosher animal?
o: Blood that spurts during the act of slaughter itself
Blood of the spleen or heart
Blood from bloodletting through which the soul departs
Blood from stabbing or maiming
quiz.e: The mishna exempts blood of the spleen, heart, eggs, and grasshoppers, since this blood is not bound up with the departure of the life-force, unlike slaughter blood, stabbing/maiming blood, or blood from lethal bloodletting.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's derivation, why is human blood excluded from the Torah's prohibition against consuming blood, despite the broad phrase 'you shall consume no manner of blood'?
o: Because humans cannot become ritually impure at all
Because the verse's comparison to 'bird or animal' requires the capacity for BOTH light and severe ritual impurity, and a human body lacks the light 'food' impurity that applies to birds and animals
Because human blood was never actually blood
Because the prohibition applies only to Temple offerings
quiz.e: The Gemara derives that the prohibition applies only to creatures sharing birds' and animals' defining traits — including the capacity for both light (food-related) and severe (corpse) impurity — and since a human body never carries the light food-impurity, human blood is excluded.
